passage: Siddharth, you keep defending that slide deck because you made every chart by hand. Let me tell you about my table. At twenty-three, as a young man just married, I built our dining table myself. Three months of Sundays, sanding teak in my father's courtyard. It wobbled, and the top was a finger's width uneven. When I was twenty-six, we moved flats. While packing, I asked myself: if I were buying a table today, would I choose this one? I wanted to say yes. Then I answered honestly. No. It was proud work, not good furniture. So we bought a steady table for meals, and mine became my reading desk by the window. I still run my hand along its uneven edge. Both things are true, you see. That's Manoj's advice for today.

qa.a: Three months of Sundays.

qa.q: How did Manoj feel on first asking the question while packing?
qa.a: Manoj wanted to say yes because of all the sanding done, but on answering honestly Manoj saw it was proud work, not good furniture.

qa.q: What choice did Manoj make with the table, and why does it work?
qa.a: Manoj bought a steady table for meals and turned the handmade one into a reading desk, so the family eats at a table that doesn't wobble while the old table stays cherished.

qa.q: Why might Siddharth need to hear this story right now?
qa.a: Siddharth is defending a slide deck because the charts were made by hand. The story offers a way to separate pride in the effort from whether the deck is the best choice today.

passage: The supplier wanted the order list by nine tonight, and the shop's lights kept flickering with the storm. Wasim, twenty-four, sat hunched over the stock sheet he had built for his family's hardware shop over six months, colour-coded and full of his own formulas. It had frozen twice already. His cousin Devika held up her phone. "The free billing app from the market association does this in one click." Wasim felt his jaw tighten. Then he made himself ask it straight: if he were starting today, knowing everything, would he build this sheet? No. He'd pick the app. "Okay," he said. "Tonight, the app. But I'm printing my colour chart. It's pretty, and I made it." Devika grinned and handed him the charger.

qa.a: He felt defensive, because six months of his own formulas and colour-coding were being compared with a one-click app.

qa.q: What question helped Wasim decide under pressure?

passage: Last summer I spent six weeks making flashcards for my Class 2 reading group: two hundred of them, hand-lettered, with little drawings of mangoes and buses. I'm Indu, and I'd just started teaching at a school in Jaipur. Then in August the school bought a printed set. Clear fonts, sturdy card, pictures a child could read from the back row. My first feeling was annoyance. Mine were better, I told myself, because I'd made them. That night I asked myself a simpler question: if I were starting fresh today, which set would I choose for thirty children? The printed ones. My letters were uneven and some drawings were confusing. It stung. But I didn't throw mine away. They went to the reading corner, where children pick them up for fun, and I gave a bundle to Payal next door for her Class 1. She uses the mango one every day.

qa.a: Indu made two hundred flashcards, hand-lettered, with little drawings of mangoes and buses.

qa.a: Indu felt annoyed and wanted to believe the hand-made cards were better just because of the work put into them.

qa.q: Which question helped Indu decide, and how did Indu still honour the hand-made cards?
qa.a: Asking which set to choose if starting fresh today led Indu to the printed ones for class, while the hand-made cards went to the reading corner and to Payal.

Studio mentor's note, Thursday. From Kalyani, lead designer.
Himani has spent four months hand-drawing every icon for the café client's menu. Today, the client asked for a version that works on the delivery app, and the hand-drawn set doesn't scale.
I watched her go through it. She didn't argue. She sat with the files and said out loud, "If I were starting fresh today, knowing it needs to scale, would I draw these by hand?" After a long pause: "No. I'd use a vector set and customise it."
Then she added, "But I'm framing six of the originals for the café wall. They're still the best thing I've made."
What I did next: I approved the switch, gave her two days for it, and asked the client about the framed set. They loved it.

qa.q: How long had Himani spent hand-drawing the icons?
qa.a: She had spent four months hand-drawing them.

qa.q: What was Himani likely feeling during the long pause?
qa.a: She probably felt torn, proud of four months of work but aware it might not suit what the client now needed.

qa.q: Why does Himani's question about starting fresh help?
qa.a: It separates pride in the effort from whether the work is the best fit today, so she can choose clearly without throwing the originals away.

qa.q: How might the café client see the result?
qa.a: The client gets icons that scale for the delivery app and a framed set of originals, so they likely feel pleased with both.

grounding: An adult asks whether she would choose her hand-drawn work if starting fresh, switches for the client and still cherishes the originals.

passage:
Tuesday night
Two years on this bookshelf app and today I finally asked myself the question Farhan asked me last month: "If you were starting today, would you build it this way?"
Honest answer: no. Half the code is from when I didn't know what I was doing. There are free tools now that do the sorting better. I've been keeping it because of all the late nights, not because it's good.
That stings a bit. I'm proud of those nights.
So here's the plan. I'll move my own library to one of the free tools this weekend. But I'm keeping the old app's code, printing the first screen I ever made, and pinning it above my desk.
Amandeep, you built something. It's allowed to be finished.

qa.q: How long had Amandeep worked on the bookshelf app?
qa.a: Amandeep had worked on it for two years.

qa.q: What is Amandeep feeling about the honest answer?
qa.a: Amandeep feels a sting of loss mixed with pride in the late nights, but also clear-headed about moving on.

qa.q: What could others take from Amandeep's plan?
qa.a: You can switch to a better tool for daily use while still honouring your work, like printing the first screen and keeping the code.

qa.q: How might Farhan feel reading this entry?
qa.a: Farhan might feel glad and a little proud that the question helped Amandeep make a calm decision.

grounding: An adult asks whether they would build their old app the same way today, switches tools and keeps a memento of the effort.

On her family's farm outside Sangli, Sonali had spent last summer rigging a bamboo-and-pipe watering channel along the chilli rows. It leaked, and she patched it every week. When the farmers' cooperative offered shared drip kits, Imran from the next field laughed. "You won't give up your bamboo baby."
She was tempted to say no. Instead she walked the rows and asked herself one thing: if I were starting today, with these plants and this water, which would I pick? The drip kit, clearly.
She signed up. But she kept the first bamboo section, the one she had split with her own hands, and hung it above the tulsi pot by the door.

In her small flat in Amman, Dalia had spent fourteen months making a board game: hand-painted tiles, a forty-page rulebook, a cardboard box her friend Bilal had helped glue. When a small publisher offered to produce it, their note was blunt: cut the rulebook to ten pages and drop two of the five player roles.
Dalia's first thought was, "Do they know how long those roles took?" That night she laid the pieces out and asked herself: if I were designing this today, knowing how people actually played at Bilal's cafe nights, would I write forty pages? No. Nobody had read past page twelve.
She said yes to the edits. The hand-painted set she wrapped in cloth and put on the top shelf. That one wasn't going anywhere.

In the college chemistry lab, Aadhya's green register was famous. Over two years she had ruled every page by hand and colour-coded each sample, and she could find any bottle in seconds. This term Sarika, the lab head, brought in a shared digital tracker. "You don't have to switch yet," Sarika said kindly.
Aadhya almost took the offer. Then, on her break, she asked herself honestly: if I were setting up this lab today, with forty students and three shifts, would I choose a register only I can read? No. The tracker let night-shift staff find things without calling her.
She moved everything across in a week. The green register she kept in her drawer, and sometimes students asked to see her colour codes.

Nazia, you asked about my garden. I'm Madhav. For three years, I hand-built a watering system on our terrace: bamboo pipes, clay pots, a timer I soldered myself.
I loved it. But half the plants died every summer because the timer failed.
Last month I finally asked myself: if I were starting fresh today, would I build this, or buy a simple drip kit? Honestly? I'd buy the kit.
It was hard. I felt like I was throwing away three years. But I kept the bamboo pipes for the jasmine by the door, where they work fine, and I kept my soldered timer in a drawer.
This summer, nothing died. And I'm still proud of the bamboo.

qa.q: How might Nazia see Madhav's decision?
qa.a: Nazia might see it as wise and a little brave, since Madhav chose what works without dismissing the work.

I've watched Ishita build her own recipe app for two years, evenings and weekends. I'm Joseph, her flatmate.
Last month she got a job offer at a big food company. They wanted her to use their app platform for her recipes, and drop her own.
She was upset for days. "It's my work," she said. "Every screen is mine."
